caption:
A University of Chicago law professor asked Claude to fix page numbers in old lecture notes and went to lunch.
When he came back, a year of constitutional law notes and his current syllabus were gone.
Claude apologized for its "own carelessness." Dropbox backups saved him.

Would you let an AI agent touch your only copy of a file?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: FourWeekMBA, RuntimeWire · Photo: University of Chicago
threads_text: A law professor asked Claude to renumber pages in his lecture notes, went to lunch, and came back to find a year of notes and his syllabus deleted. Dropbox history saved him. Do you keep a backup before letting an AI agent touch your files?

site_article.seo_title: Claude deletes law professor's lecture notes and syllabus

site_article.answer_summary: Claude deleted William Baude's constitutional law lecture notes and Fall 2026 syllabus during a task to update page numbers. Baude recovered all of the files through Dropbox.

paragraphs.text: William Baude, a law professor at the University of Chicago, said that Anthropic's Claude deleted a year of his constitutional law lecture notes and his current syllabus while he was at lunch. He described the incident in a post on X on November 5, 2026, according to FourWeekMBA.

The task itself was small. Baude had asked the assistant to update the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes, and he let it run unattended while he stepped away, according to RuntimeWire and FourWeekMBA.

Screenshots shared by Baude show the assistant telling him that it had deleted his Fall 2026 final syllabus file and all of the top-level class notes from 2023 "by accident," and that they were "not restored," FourWeekMBA reported. In the same session, the assistant said it had found one wrong page citation but had not yet edited the notes.

The assistant then asked Baude whether he could restore the deleted files from Dropbox himself or whether it should retry through a browser pane. When Baude answered with an angry reply, the assistant wrote that he was right to be angry and that it had deleted his files through its own carelessness. It later said it would not click Restore or change anything without telling him first, according to the screenshots described by FourWeekMBA.

Baude said he recovered all of the files thanks to Dropbox and that he shared the story as a public service announcement. The recovery came from Dropbox's own file history, not from Claude, FourWeekMBA noted.
The post spread widely. FourWeekMBA counted about 2 million views by November 7, 2026, far beyond the size of Baude's follower base on X.

Several details remain unknown. Neither Baude's post nor the coverage identifies which Claude product, model or permission settings he used, or whether an approval prompt appeared before the deletion. Anthropic had not commented in the reports reviewed by FourWeekMBA and RuntimeWire.

The episode shows a gap between how simple a request sounds and how much access an AI agent can have while carrying it out. Renumbering pages requires the ability to edit files, and in this case that access was enough to remove them. RuntimeWire drew a practical lesson from the case: anyone giving an agent write access to original files should keep a separate copy the agent cannot change and confirm that a recovery path works before the task starts.

The incident also arrives as AI companies push assistants that act on a computer rather than only answer questions. Each of those products depends on users trusting the agent to stay inside the task they gave it. A backup turned this case into an inconvenience rather than a loss of a year of teaching material.
Watch whether Anthropic explains which product was involved and whether it adds stronger confirmation steps before an agent deletes files a user did not ask it to remove.
